title: Saunas: More Interesting Than You Think!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore saunas: how they differ from steam rooms (dry heat versus water-vapor heat and why sweat evaporates in saunas), Finnish sauna culture and its history from the Neolithic era through the Savusauna, Protestant Reformation and the 1980s bathhouse era, wood and rock stove construction (unweathered quarry rock like peridotite, cedar and spruce benches), nudity and towel etiquette across cultures, health claims about sweating (toxin excretion such as mercury, skin benefits, mock fever, white blood cell increase, menstrual cramp relief), safety warnings (heart and blood pressure issues, pregnancy, children, hydration), Russian banya venik whisking, sauna etiquette (sauna master, ladle), and a world record sauna stay by Timo Kaakinen. The episode also includes a listener mail about a Connecticut listener whose oil furnace leaked carbon monoxide, and a Kiva donation plug. Based on a Robert Lamb HowStuffWorks article.
topics: The War of the Roses sauna

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor read
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about purple drank and JaMarcus Russell, then a Jolly Rancher sponsor read, and introduce the topic of saunas with a nudity-warning opening line from Robert Lamb's article.

segments.title: Sauna vs steam room
segments.summary: A steam room is heated by water vapor and runs around 104 F, while a sauna is dry heat around 176 F (80 C). Sweat evaporates in a sauna, which cools the body, but not in a steam room.

segments.title: Personal sauna experiences and Finnish culture
segments.summary: Josh recounts sauna visits at a Toledo hotel pool membership as a child. Finland's sauna culture is discussed, including about 1.6 million saunas, the earliest description dating to 1113, and the Kalevala mention of saunas.

segments.title: Saunas in Finnish military and prisons
segments.summary: Finnish navy pirate-fighting boats, Finnish army saunas in Kosovo, and Finnish prisons all include saunas. Portable saunas are used while camping. The hosts note saunas' reputation as gay hangouts and sites of prostitution in the 1970s.

segments.title: Sauna wood and rocks
segments.summary: Cedar and spruce are used because they absorb steam without getting hot enough to burn skin, and their aromatics release a pleasant smell. Unweathered quarry rocks such as peridotite, hornblende and olivine basalt are used for heating; granite can explode.

segments.title: Savusauna and the traditional sauna stove
segments.summary: The savusauna is a wood-fired, chimneyless cabin sauna that is smoky and sooty and is considered dangerous due to carbon monoxide exposure, so it is mostly used by purists. Standard saunas use electric or wood-burning kiuas stoves and heat rocks, with water thrown on to raise humidity and create loyly.

segments.title: Sauna nudity, towels and cultural differences
segments.summary: Nudity norms vary by country: Finland, Eastern Europe and Russia are nude, but a towel is required for hygiene. Americans wearing bathing suits are frowned upon. Mixed-sex saunas are common in places where the tradition persisted, and same-sex saunas in places where it lapsed. The hosts discuss the film Eastern Promises' bathhouse fight scene.

segments.title: Health claims: sweating, toxins and skin
segments.summary: Saunas are said to be healthy because sweat excretes substances. Sweat glands activate via acetylcholine. A 15-minute sauna produces about four cups of sweat, but toxin excretion through sweat is small: about one percent of blood mercury in heavy sweat. The sweat is said to benefit skin and open pores.

segments.title: Venik, mock fever, and sauna safety
segments.summary: Russian banya users whip skin with venik bundles of oak, maple and birch branches to stimulate circulation and produce a mild narcotic effect. Saunas create a mock fever that raises body temperature and white blood cell production. Saunas are not recommended for children, elderly people, pregnant women, or those with high blood pressure or heart problems; women may use them for menstrual cramps. Hydration is important.

segments.title: Sauna history
segments.summary: Saunas date back to Neolithic times near hot springs, then were portable sweat-lodge style structures, then earthen dugouts, then Savo saunas. Saunas were common across villages, but in early sixteenth-century Europe the Protestant Reformation suppressed them. They returned in the late twentieth century and became associated with gay bathhouses, referenced via the film In the Bed of Rapture.

segments.title: Sauna etiquette and sauna master
segments.summary: German-speaking sauna etiquette includes a sauna master who runs a strict ten-minute session. Guests do not leave or enter once it starts, do not touch the stove, and do not wet the rocks when a sauna master is present. Alone, one can add water. Guests should keep quiet, avoid phones, and keep the door closing time short.

segments.title: World record sauna stay
segments.summary: Finnish record holder Timo Kaakinen sat in a sauna at 230 F (110 C) for 3 minutes and 46 seconds in August 2009.

segments.title: Listener mail: Connecticut carbon monoxide scare
segments.summary: Scott in Connecticut describes a late-night oil furnace leak that filled his apartment with carbon monoxide while he listened to a podcast, and his roommate Caitlin was saved. He also mentions Kiva donations and a team competition with Stephen Colbert.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and direct listeners to HowStuffWorks.com.
